speaker: Anna Lembke
title: Overcome Addictions and Obsessions of All Kinds | Dr. Anna Lembke
question: In psychiatric and pain medicine, why do patients with legitimate medical conditions still develop severe addiction to prescribed medications like ketamine?
guest: We see people get very addicted to ketamine, get it from the black market, use very large amounts, and end up with very severe psychological and neurological problems. We also see people who have no business using ketamine to treat depression because of their addiction diathesis and their past addiction to ketamine, who then find a ketamine provider, and either they don't tell that person that they've been addicted to ketamine, or that person doesn't ask, and then they end up getting ketamine in that setting, and that sets them off. Anytime a doctor is prescribing any addictive substance for any illness at all, we must keep in mind that just because an individual has an illness that might indicate that addictive substance doesn't make that individual immune to getting addicted. This was the big myth with the opioid epidemic: as long as you are being prescribed opioids for pain, you're somehow immune to the problem of addiction. Absolutely false. The same is true for any addictive substance, whether it's Xanax for anxiety, ketamine for depression, or stimulants for ADHD. You can have all of those bona fide conditions and still get addicted to the medication you're being prescribed to treat that condition.

points.core: Having a bona fide medical diagnosis provides zero immunity against medication addiction.
points.note: Accept: a legitimate clinical indication (pain, depression, anxiety, ADHD) does not protect patients from becoming addicted to prescribed controlled substances. Do not credit: claiming only recreational users get addicted or generic warnings that "all drugs have side effects."

points.core: Addiction-prone patients obtain risky prescriptions when prescribers fail to screen past histories.
points.note: Accept: patients with addiction diathesis or prior addiction omitting their history or clinicians failing to ask/screen before prescribing. Do not credit: blaming patients alone without noting screening/prescribing gaps, or generic calls for "better healthcare."

points.core: Clinical exposure in vulnerable patients can trigger relapse into high-dose illicit escalation.
points.note: Accept: medically administered exposure setting off relapse, black-market escalation, or severe neurological/psychiatric harm. Do not credit: asserting therapeutic ketamine is completely safe or completely useless.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Having a legitimate medical condition does not protect the brain from the pharmacology of a reinforcing drug. Ketamine, opioids, and benzodiazepines act on reward and stress circuits regardless of why they are taken, so repeated exposure can produce tolerance, craving, and compulsive use in anyone.

Several factors compound the risk in these patients. Chronic pain, depression, and trauma are themselves risk factors for addiction, since they share neurobiology with it, such as dysregulated reward and stress systems. The drug also relieves real suffering, which is a powerful negative reinforcer: patients learn that the medication removes distress, and as tolerance shortens or weakens the benefit, they escalate dose or frequency. Ketamine's dissociative and euphoric effects add direct positive reinforcement, and its antidepressant effect fades within days, encouraging repeat dosing.

System factors matter too: at-home or loosely monitored prescribing, inadequate screening for prior substance use, and no clear plan for stopping.

Most patients treated under supervised protocols do not develop addiction, but when it occurs with ketamine it can be severe, including bladder damage and cognitive impairment.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
A legitimate medical diagnosis does not shield the brain from a drug’s neurobiology. Medications like ketamine act rapidly on reward and stress pathways—blocking NMDA receptors while triggering downstream dopamine surges and engaging endogenous opioid signaling—which reinforces repeated use regardless of why treatment began.

In psychiatric and pain patients, fast relief from debilitating depression, trauma, or chronic pain also creates powerful negative reinforcement. Because ketamine’s acute analgesic, anxiolytic, and dissociative effects wear off quickly, returning symptoms and withdrawal-like rebound distress can blur the line between therapeutic redosing and compulsive craving. Rapid pharmacological tolerance further drives dose escalation, gradually reshaping prefrontal and striatal circuits that govern executive function and impulse control.

Underlying vulnerability compounds this risk: chronic pain, treatment-resistant mood disorders, and substance use disorders share overlapping genetic and neurobiological pathways, including baseline reward-deficit and stress-system dysregulation. Finally, prescribing context matters. When treatment shifts from infrequent, closely supervised clinic infusions to frequent or loosely monitored at-home regimens, repeated high-frequency exposure accelerates tolerance and psychological dependence, leading to loss of control even in patients who sought only symptom relief.

noweb.answer: Patients with legitimate medical conditions can develop severe addiction because the brain’s reward circuitry responds to a drug’s neurochemical effects regardless of therapeutic intent. Ketamine acts rapidly on glutamate and downstream dopamine and opioid pathways, producing not only analgesia and antidepressant effects, but also euphoria, calm, and dissociation. For someone enduring chronic pain or severe psychiatric distress, this fast-acting relief creates powerful negative reinforcement, conditioning the brain to seek the drug as an immediate escape from suffering. With repeated or frequent exposure, neuroadaptation sets in: rapid tolerance blunts clinical efficacy, while rebound pain, anxiety, or dysphoria between doses mimics a worsening of the underlying illness. Seeking to recapture relief, patients may escalate their dose or frequency, gradually shifting behavioral control from conscious medical use to compulsive, habit-driven neural circuits. Individual vulnerabilities—such as genetic predisposition, trauma history, prior substance use disorders, or loosely supervised at-home prescribing with frequent dosing—further accelerate this transition, turning a genuinely needed therapy into severe addiction despite mounting physical and psychological harm.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Having a real condition doesn't protect anyone from addiction, because addiction comes from how the drug acts on the brain, not from why it was prescribed. Ketamine strongly reinforces its own use. It produces fast relief, dissociation and euphoria, and its antidepressant effect often fades within days. That creates a cycle of relief and relapse that pushes people to take it more often or at higher doses. Tolerance builds quickly, so the same dose stops working.

Vulnerability plays a large part. Depression, PTSD and chronic pain overlap heavily with trauma, past substance use and genetic risk. Some patients come to rely on the drug to escape distress rather than to treat their illness. Prescribing practices add to the risk. Take-home lozenges or nasal sprays, telehealth prescribing with little monitoring, and loose dose limits remove the safeguards of supervised clinic dosing, which is why esketamine (Spravato) must be given under observation.

Prescribers may also miss early warning signs, such as asking for refills early or saying the drug feels essential, because the original use was legitimate. Heavy, long-term use can also cause bladder damage (ketamine cystitis) and memory problems.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Having a legitimate medical condition does not insulate the brain from a drug’s underlying neurobiology. Medications like ketamine act on glutamate, opioid, and dopamine-related pathways that regulate both pain and reward, producing rapid relief from severe physical or emotional distress alongside dissociation or euphoria. This creates powerful positive and negative reinforcement: patients learn quickly that the drug not only feels rewarding but also immediately silences suffering. With repeated exposure, the brain adapts, leading to tolerance—where escalating doses are needed for the same relief—and rebound symptoms or distress when the medication wears off. Furthermore, people treated for severe depression, trauma, or chronic pain frequently carry preexisting vulnerability factors for substance use disorders, including genetic predisposition, chronic stress, and limited alternative relief. When prescribing involves frequent dosing, take-home access, or insufficient monitoring, therapeutic use can gradually cross into compulsive drug-seeking, loss of control, and severe addiction despite its legitimate clinical origins.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A medication can relieve a real medical condition and still reinforce repeated use. Ketamine can rapidly ease pain or depression, and its dissociative or sometimes euphoric effects can also feel rewarding. When relief fades and symptoms return, some patients begin to crave the drug or take it more often than prescribed. With repeated use, tolerance can develop, so the same dose has less effect. Persistent symptoms, frequent access to the medication, and a history of substance use problems can increase the risk.

Tolerance alone doesn’t establish addiction. Addiction involves impaired control, such as repeatedly taking more than intended or continuing to use despite serious harm. A patient can reach that point even if they started treatment exactly as prescribed and still have a legitimate need for pain or psychiatric care.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A legitimate medical need and an addiction can coexist. Ketamine can relieve pain or depression, and that relief can reinforce the urge to take it again. Some people also find its dissociative effects rewarding. With repeated use, especially at higher doses or more often than prescribed, some people develop tolerance and cravings. As the effects wear off and distress returns, a person may start taking doses closer together and find it increasingly difficult to stop, even when use is causing harm.

Wanting relief, developing tolerance, or having symptoms return between treatments does not by itself mean someone has an addiction. The hallmark is impaired control over use despite harmful consequences. Risk varies with dose, frequency, access, and individual vulnerability, including a history of substance use problems. Clinical monitoring can reduce that risk, and someone who develops an addiction still deserves treatment for the pain or depression that led them to seek care.
